newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian voters flock to Hanson's "One Nation".
newsitem.headline: Australian voters flock to Hanson's "One Nation".

text.p: A new party founded by Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson has proved a hit with voters and become the country's third political force in just two weeks, according to a poll published on Tuesday.
The Morgan poll said that "Pauline Hanson's One Nation" party, founded by the independent Queensland MP this month, would already attract 10 percent of first-preference votes.
"We are creating Australian political history -- this is the biggest threat to established parties," party director David Ettridge told Reuters from One Nation's Sydney headquarters.
"It's a frustration vote. It's a complete abandonment of long-held, traditional political support."

The poll will come as a blow to Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal-National coalition, which polled only 40 percent of first-preference votes in its worst performance since before the March 1996 election which brought it to power.
The coalition's lead over the opposition Labor party was only 5.5 points, also its lowest since the election, showing that voters were deserting Howard for Hanson.
The Australian Democrats, traditionally the third force in Australian politics, enjoyed only 7.5 percent support according to the poll of 1,085 voters.

Hanson, a red-headed former fish-and-chip-shop owner from Queensland, was elected as an independent in what had been viewed as a safe Labor seat after being disowned by Howard's Liberal party for views seen as racist.

She made her maiden speech last September, creating a storm by complaining that the country risked being swamped by Asian immigrants and Aboriginal welfare was putting white Australians at a disadvantage.
The ensuing race row, which made headlines in Asia and beyond, left mainstream political parties wrong-footed as polls showed voters supported Hanson on immigration.
Howard himself was widely criticised for not repudiating Hanson forcefully or quickly enough.

Ettridge, a former fund-raiser for Third World charities, said he thought the party's success was not just a passing phenomenon and it could be registering 30 or 40 percent support by the next election -- despite a row over a book bearing Hanson's name accusing some Aboriginal tribes of cannibalism.
In two weeks the party had already used up its first batch of 10,000 membership application forms and was receiving non-stop calls from potential members, Ettridge added.
"Australians have taken to Pauline in a very affectionate way," he said. "Pauline speaks the truth, even if she speaks without the great intellect of the scholars in parliament."
Hanson's party nevertheless faces various legal challenges before it can get off the ground and field electoral candidates.
The Australian Electoral Commission said on Tuesday it had received 77 formal submissions for the party's registration to be blocked.
Those trying to block the party included Aboriginal, Chinese, Islamic, Holocaust survivors and other groups, as well as individuals offended by her choice of party name.

"The concept of a nation or nationhood belongs to the Australian people. It does not belong to Pauline Hanson," one Sydney man wrote in a submission to the commission. A Brisbane voter told the commission: "Divided Nation may be a more appropriate label."
